content: As maternal treatment programs expand and mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) rates decline, the likelihood of false-positive results in HIV testing is expected to increase. Therefore, it is critical to perform a confirmatory test following an initial positive nucleic acid test (NAT) to prevent unnecessary treatment, especially in settings with low transmission rates. If the second test yields a negative result, a third NAT should be conducted before discontinuing antiretroviral therapy (ART). For children who have never been breastfed, additional testing is recommended after a negative NAT at 4–6 weeks of age to account for the possibility of false-negative results. The risk of HIV transmission persists as long as breastfeeding continues. If a test is conducted at 9 months but less than 3 months after breastfeeding cessation, infections acquired during the final days of breastfeeding may be missed. Retesting at 18 months or 3 months after breastfeeding cessation (whichever is later) is necessary for a definitive assessment of HIV status. If breastfeeding extends beyond 18 months, the final diagnosis of HIV status can only be determined at the end of breastfeeding. If breastfeeding ends before 18 months, antibody testing at 18 months is required for a conclusive diagnosis, provided it is conducted at least 3 months after breastfeeding cessation to allow for the development of HIV antibodies. For infants under 18 months, NAT should be used to confirm infection. For infants older than 18 months, a negative antibody test confirms the absence of infection, while a positive antibody test confirms infection. Programs must ensure that all HIV-exposed infants are retained in care and tested appropriately throughout the exposure period. Infants with positive test results must undergo confirmatory testing. Those with repeatedly indeterminate results should be actively tracked, retained in care, and retested until their status is resolved. ART programs should prioritize confirmatory testing of all positive and indeterminate results using a new sample. Clinical monitoring and further testing should follow national infant testing schedules until a definitive HIV status is established. Declining global MTCT rates have raised concerns about false-positive and indeterminate test results. Individuals with indeterminate results require immediate repeat testing and management according to standard operating procedures. A multidisciplinary team of healthcare providers is essential for supporting retention, tracking, and resolving the status of individuals with repeated indeterminate results. Point-of-care (POC) nucleic acid testing is recommended for diagnosing HIV in infants and children under 18 months of age. This approach has demonstrated high certainty in evidence and significantly improves patient outcomes compared to laboratory-based technologies. POC testing reduces the time to deliver results to caregivers, with same-day results achieved in 97% of cases compared to 0% with standard care. The median time from sample collection to caregivers receiving results was 0 days for POC testing versus 35 days for standard care. Additionally, 51% of infants living with HIV initiated ART on the same day as sample collection with POC testing, compared to 0% with standard care. Cost-effectiveness analyses have shown that POC testing is more cost-effective than standard care, particularly when devices are shared across disease programs such as tuberculosis and HIV. In Zambia, for example, POC testing saved $752 per additional person initiating ART when devices were shared. Current POC infant diagnosis tests cost $15–25 per test, with instruments costing approximately $15,000. Expanding access to POC testing in high-burden countries could significantly increase the number of infants initiating ART, with costs ranging from $325 to $622 per additional person initiating treatment. Ethically, cost concerns should not hinder the adoption of POC testing if clinical and public health evidence supports its use. Collaboration with international agencies and diagnostic companies is necessary to reduce costs and ensure widespread availability. Community engagement is also critical to increase acceptance and demand for POC testing. Studies have shown that reduced time to receive test results alleviates caregiver anxiety and enables earlier treatment initiation. Caregivers generally trust POC testing results, particularly printed results, which are perceived as less prone to human error. However, some caregivers expressed skepticism about results generated too quickly. Overall, caregivers and healthcare workers support POC testing, with most respondents confident in its feasibility and acceptability.
